Executive Summary
ES-05 Executive Summary – 24 CFR 91.200(c), 91.220(b)
1. Introduction
As a HUD-defined Urban County1, the County of Santa Clara (County) receives federal block grant funding
from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) annually. These funds include the
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and the HOME Investment Partnerships Program (HOME)—
and are used to address a variety of unmet housing, supportive service, and community development
needs.
CDBG funds are allocated within the Urban County geographic area, which includes the unincorporated
county and the Cities of Campbell, Los Altos, Los Altos Hills, Los Gatos, Monte Sereno, Morgan Hill, and
Saratoga. HOME funds are allocated to HOME Consortium cities, which include Cupertino, Gilroy, Palo
Alto, and the Urban County.
Annually, the County of Santa Clara receives approximately $1.5 million in CDBG funds; over the five-year
planning period this approximates $7.25 million. In the past, CDBG has been used for a variety of programs
that provide critical services to low-income households in the small cities and unincorporated areas of the
County. Historically, CDBG has been used for:
• Public services, or supportive services, that provide direct support to low-income individuals and
households in need of assistance;
• Housing rehabilitation to low-income homeowners who cannot afford improvements on their own
including improvements that are needed to remain in their homes and age in place;
• Acquisition, disposition, and clearance of land to create affordable housing; and
• Construction of and improvements to public and community facilities.
The County anticipates receiving approximately $850,000 annually and $4,150,000 in HOME funds in the
next five years. HOME funding is dedicated to creating and preserving affordable housing.
To receive these funds from HUD, the County is required to prepare a Consolidated Plan every five years,
which identifies the County’s priority housing and community development needs and goals in the Urban
County geographic area. This is that plan. It covers five program years (PY) from 2025 through 2030.
This Consolidated Plan was developed through analysis of current housing market data; an assessment of
the housing and supportive service needs of low - and moderate-income (LMI) populations; stakeholder
and resident consultations through focus groups and community meetings; and a resident survey. The
County of Santa Clara led a cooperative effort to prepare the Consolidated Plan with entitlement
jurisdictions and HOME Consortium members.
The Consolidated Plan is implemented through the Urban County’s Annual Action Plans (“Annual Action
Plan”), which identifies how annual funding allocations are invested to achieve identified priorities and
goals. The Consolidated Annual Performance Evaluation Report (CAPER) reports how funding was
1 HUD’s definition of Urban County is a county with a population of more than 200,000 excluding “entitlement” communities which receive
CDBG directly. The HOME program Consortium is comprised of cities within the county that do not receive HOME directly.
allocated and outcomes achieved through block grant investments annually.
PRIORITY NEEDS for the FIVE-YEAR PLANNING PERIOD
The research conducted to support the Consolidated Plan helps identify the most critical needs of low-
and moderate-income residents. The priority needs developed from this Plan include:
• Affordable and supportive housing for extremely low -income, unhoused, and similar specific
populations with acute housing needs;
• Supportive services to respond to and prevent homelessness;
• Affordable and emergency housing and assistance for families escaping domestic violence; and
• Supportive services to assist low-income and special needs populations with economic and housing
stability.
• Improvements to aging community facilities and public infrastructure.
FIVE-YEAR GOALS that will GUIDE ANNUAL INVESTMENTS
Priority needs inform the five -year Consolidated plan goals, which guide annual funding allocations. The
five-year goals for the Urban County include:
• Increase affordable and supportive housing;
• Preserve existing affordable and supportive housing;
• Provide essential services for special needs residents, including those escaping domestic violence;
• Maintain and expand activities designed to ensure housing stability and prevent and reduce
homelessness;
• Invest in improvements and development of public facilities and support economic resiliency
activities as opportunities arise.
2. Summary of the objectives and outcomes identified in the Plan
The Urban County anticipates achieving the following objectives and outcomes through CDBG and HOME
investments:
• Stabilize households at-risk of homelessness to reduce the risk of homelessness;
• Provide critical supportive services to individuals and households who are extremely to very low-
income and have special needs;
• Construct new, and preserve existing, affordable and supportive housing;
• Make needed infrastructure improvements that benefit low- and moderate-income households.
3. Evaluation of past performance
The County is responsible for ensuring compliance with all rules and regulations associated with the CDBG
and HOME programs. The County recognizes that the evaluation of past performance is critical to ensuring
that its subrecipients are implementing activities effectively and those activities align with the Urban
County’s overall strategies and goals.
Over the last five years of the previous Consolidated Plan cycle, the County has programmed
approximately $7 million in CDBG funding and $3.8 million in HOME funds to advance the goals and
strategies previously identified. Accomplishments include:
• $1 million of CDBG funding was spent to support 7,422 persons receiving essential services relating
to affordable housing for special needs populations
• $2.3 million of CDBG funds and $2.3 million of HOME funds were used toward construction of 203
new rental units along with 132 beds created for people experiencing homelessness
• $800,000 of CDBG funds were allocated to maintain, improve and expand community facilities
• $2.1 million of CDBG funds and $1.5 million of HOME funding was utilized to preserve existing
affordable housing, with over 190 single family homes rehabilitated for low -income homeowners
to be able to maintain their homes
• $500,000 of CDBG funds were utilized for Public Service activities related to preventing and
reducing homelessness, serving 1079 persons and creating 589 overnight shelter beds
• $240,000 of CDBG funding was allocated to address Fair Housing needs, serving 568 persons.
4. Summary of citizen participation process and consultation process
The County of Santa Clara and the other entitlement jurisdictions coordinated stakeholder consultation
and resident engagement to leverage opportunities and minimize duplication. This engagement included:
• A Consolidated Plan website—www.letstalkhousingscc.org—with information about the Planning
process including a short video and presentation; a link to the resident survey and activities to
prioritize housing and community development needs; and community r esources. The website
contains a translation feature for easy conversion into multiple languages.
• A community survey, available between October and December 2024, and promoted through
supportive service and public agencies that work with low - and moderate-income residents, city
social media, and the Consolidated Plan website.
• Creation of a social media and communications toolkit with materials for jurisdictions to promote
public participation activities and provide information to share through social media channels like
NextDoor, Facebook, and Let’s Talk Housing SCC.
• A presentation about the Consolidated Plan and opportunity to provide input on funding priorities
at the Lived Experience Advisory Board of Silicon Valley (LEAB) monthly meeting.
• Two virtual regional workshops open to all residents living in and stakeholders serving residents in
the County. The workshops included a brief overview about the Planning process, simple activities
to express priority needs, and in-depth discussions about needs in breakout rooms.
• Pop-up engagement in the Urban County and entitlement jurisdictions. For the Urban County,
engagement occurred at the Farmers Market in Campbell in December 2024 and at the Saratoga
Library in November 2024 . Residents attending the Farmers Market were invited to engage in
hands-on activities to identify priority needs for the Consolidated Plan. Staff talked with around 40
people in the community including youth, seniors, families, and more. Residents were encouraged
to interact with the comment boards by sharing examples of community improvements they would
like to see funded through the Consolidated Plan. Residents were also directed to the online survey
to provide additional feedback and suggestions. Staff emphasized the importance of capturing
community input and assured attendees that their feedback would be shared with the County and
applicable cities.
• Three focus groups with stakeholders in housing, supportive services, and community
development serving residents throughout the c ounty. After a brief presentation about the
Consolidated Plan process —including information on how to circulate the survey and
letstalkhousingscc.org website to clients—stakeholders participated in in-depth discussion about
priority needs and solutions to needs . Attendees represented affordable housing providers ,
service providers serving special needs populations, people with lived experience of
homelessness, legal advocates, childcare service providers, public health agencies, mental health
service providers, and others.
• One-on-one interviews with staff of the Continuum of Care (CoC), which receives HOPWA and ESG
funding and distributes that funding to the County’s public service departments.
• One-on-one interviews with Urban County jurisdiction economic development professionals and
nonprofits who provide economic development and job training and skill development services.
• One-on-one interviews with the Santa Clara County Housing Authority, the local public housing
authority which serves all of Santa Clara County.
5. Summary of public comments
All public comments received were provided to HUD as an attached document in the administrative
section of IDIS. Seven representatives of nonprofit organizations provided public comment in support of
their operations at the April 4 th public hearing at the Housing and Community Development Advisory
Committee (HCDAC) meeting, and 1 community member provided comment expressing concern for
funding in Los Altos. Three representatives from nonprofit organizations provided public comment in
support of their operations at the June 3rd public hearing held at the Board of Supervisors meeting, and 1
resident provided public comment regarding County staff communications. Three public comments were
received through the Let’s Talk Housing website addressing the need for affordable housing and
requesting prioritization of housing for survivors of domestic violence. These comments are also provided
in the Public Comments and Notices document.
No additional public comments were received regarding the Consolidated Plan.
6. Summary of comments or views not accepted and the reasons for not accepting them
All comments were accepted and considered in development of the Plan.

Narrative
The County of Santa Clara administers CDBG on behalf of the unincorporated areas of the County, in
addition to seven small jurisdictions: the C ities of Campbell, Los Altos, Los Altos Hills, Los Gatos, Monte
Sereno, Morgan Hill, and Saratoga, also known as the “Urban County” program. In 2015, the County
entered into a HOME Consortium with the Urban County cities and the cities of Cupertino, Gilroy , and
Palo Alto and serves as the administrator of HOME funds for the unincorporated County and these cities.
The J oint Powers Authority (JPA) for both CDBG and HOME were most recently updated in 2023 to
continue these partnerships. This Consolidated Plan presents data for the County overall, for the Urban
County (County less CDBG entitlement community data), and for the Urban County plus HOME
Consortium.

Introduction
Provide a concise summary of the jurisdiction’s activities to enhance coordination between public and
assisted housing providers and private and governmental health, mental health and service agencies
The County of Santa Cla ra’s Office of Supportive Housing (OSH) is the County’s coordinating body for all
housing and community development work and manages the County’s supportive housing and
homelessness prevention systems, which serve those experiencing or at -risk of homelessness,
respectively. OSH also oversees the Continuum of Care (CoC). In these roles, OSH:
• Implements community-wide efforts to end homelessness and monitors programmatic coverage,
efficiency, and effectiveness;
• Manages the Pedro Street interim housing center, which provides short term shelter and
connections to medical and social services for residents experiencing homelessness while they wait
for intake, evaluation, and housing assistance;
• Supports the Here4You call center hotline that centralizes referrals for clients needing shelter in
Santa Clara County;
• Holds monthly meetings with city housing staff to discuss project coordination;
• Connects local staff with resources and best practices; and
• Oversees the implementation of the $950 million 2016 Housing Bond Affordable Housing Bond
(Housing Bond). To date, the County has approved over $700,000,000 towards 57 affordable and
supportive housing developments across 11 cities in the county, representing 5,749 total
units. When all developments are in operation, the County and its partners will have created new
permanent housing opportunities for approximately 17,100 people, with 43% of units set-aside for
previously unhoused individuals and family members.
Describe coordination with the Continuum of Care and efforts to address the needs of homeless persons
(particularly chronically homeless individuals and families, families with children, veterans, and
unaccompanied youth) and persons at risk of homelessness
The Continuum of Care (CoC) is a multi-sector group of stakeholders dedicated to ending and preventing
homelessness in the County and is overseen by the County’s OSH staff. The CoC’s primary responsibilities
are to coordinate large-scale implementation of efforts to prevent and end homelessness in the County.
Coordination between the County and the CoC to address the needs of homeless persons occurs through:
• Sharing data across safety net, criminal justice, and housing systems to better predict and target
households who are experiencing or at risk of homelessness;
• Expanding the housing supply needed for households on the CoC waiting list and in the shelter system.
This includes expanding housing programs for families involved in the child welfare system and
expanding and diversifying long-term housing options for foster youth;
• Prioritizing development of housing for extremely low-income households and monitoring regional
targets
• Ensuring that County housing policies do not create barriers to permanent supportive housing and
taking a leadership role on land use and zoning policies;
• Expanding and developing new housing and workforce development programs to successfully
integrate justice-involved residents back into the community;
• Funding legal and housing assistance programs to help households maintain housing;
• Funding street outreach, hygiene services, and transportation options to match the needs of
unsheltered residents; and
• Expanding the supportive housing system and developing programs tailored to the needs of specific
persons experiencing homelessness including youth, older adults, families with children, and veterans.
OSH is the Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) lead for the County and CoC.
The CoC works closely with the Lived Experience Advisory Board of Silicon Valley (LEAB) , Destination:
Home, and other community organizations which work collaboratively to end and prevent homelessness).
The LEAB is a leadership development body consisting of members with current or past experiences of
homelessness. LEAB members participated in the Consolidated Plan through a focus group that was part
of their monthly meetings and participation in community workshops.
Many of the CoC Board members also serve on the Destination: Home Leadership Board. Destination:
Home is a public -private partnership committed to collective impact strategies to end chronic
homelessness, serves as the backbone organization to the CoC and is responsible for implementing by -
laws and protocols that govern the operations of the CoC.
Describe consultation with the Continuum(s) of Care that serves the jurisdiction's area in determining
how to allocate ESG funds, develop performance standards and evaluate outcomes, and develop
funding, policies and procedures for the administration of HMIS
The County OSH is the Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) Lead for the County CoC. The
CoC and its HMIS system administrator vendor, Bitfocus, work to meets and exceeds HUD’s requirements
for the implementation and compliance of HMIS Data Standards. This involves overall administration,
implementation, and operation of HMIS, including providing end user training, meeting federal reporting
requirements, and continuously monitoring data quality and system performance. HMIS policies and
procedures ar e developed in accordance with HUD’s HMIS data standards. The CoC prepares annual
reports of system performance standards for: 1) the length of time homeless; 2) exits and returns to
homelessness (within 12 months and within 2 years); 3) the number of residents moved into PSH and
Rapid Rehousing; 4) employment and income growth; 5) success at reducing the number of people who
are first-time homeless; and 6) clients covered by health insurance.
